transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-12-09
Time: 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Jared Kim (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Aisha Patel (Sequoia ML - Head of ML), Tom Baker (Infra), Marta Gomez (SRE)

Summary: Quick walkthrough of Redwood Optimize quantization profiles focusing on INT8 vs FP8, showing quality vs latency graphs, and discussing a pilot on customer's H100 cluster.

[00:00] Jared: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, I think we have about 50 minutes, I'll let Priya run through the Optimize walkthrough and we'll save Qs for after each section. Aisha, thanks for inviting Tom and Marta.
[00:18] Aisha: Yeah thanks Jared, quick context - we're exploring ways to cut token cost for our real-time assistant without losing accuracy; production SLO is 300ms p95 and we run on H100s now.
[00:32] Priya: Perfect, that helps. Today I'll show INT8 and FP8 profiles, what we typically see on latency and quality, and then some knobs: batching, kv cache, and fallback routes. The deck's up in the doc I shared earlier.
[00:45] Tom: Quick Q before you start - when you say INT8 are you referring to per-tensor or per-channel quantization? We care a lot about determinism for caching.
[00:54] Priya: Good call. For our Optimize flow we default to per-channel scales for weights and mixed precision for activations; INT8 path is usually per-channel symmetric or asymmetric depending on the kernel, FP8 is a hardware-friendly 8-bit float path. Sorry if I said kernel names weird earlier in the doc - sometimes the auto transcripts call them knurlers.
[01:12] Marta: (laughs) noted.
[01:18] Priya: Alright slide 1 - baseline: float16 on H100. Baseline p95 ~ 320ms for your typical 256-token convo on the model family you're evaluating. INT8 tends to give ~1.6-2.5x throughput improvements depending on token length and batching; FP8 is often slightly lower overhead but keeps a bit more numeric fidelity. On our eval sets we typically see quality delta in the order of 0.5-1.5% depending on metric - sometimes negligible for chat-style generation, sometimes noticeable on math/long context.
[01:49] Aisha: Can you quantify 'quality delta'? We run a mix of extractive QA and summarization and care about ROUGE/EM drops more than subjective chat quality.
[02:01] Priya: Yep - in past pilots on similar models, INT8 had median ROUGE drop around 0.8% and EM drop ~1.2% on edge cases; FP8 was more like 0.2-0.6% ROUGE and 0.3-0.9% EM. Those are approximate, your mileage will vary. We always recommend the eval set pilot.
[02:28] Tom: Do those numbers come from your internal evals or public benchmarks?
[02:33] Priya: Internal bench + customer pilots. We include a per-model quantization profile - it's the Optimize output that says, ok for this model INT8 is safe for heads A,B but for heavy math workloads we fall back to fp16 for certain layers.
[02:47] Jared: And we can do conservative profiles vs aggressive ones; conservative is tuned to <0.5% quality delta typically.
[02:56] Marta: How does KV cache affect latency with these quant profiles? We use long context caching heavily.
[03:03] Priya: KV cache mostly affects memory footprint. For INT8 the KV cache size reduces proportionally so you fit longer contexts on the same GPU which indirectly reduces retrieval latencies because you avoid sharding across instances. For FP8 there are similar gains. For a lot of customers, enabling prefix KV caching plus INT8 gets p95 from ~320ms to ~210-240ms on H100. If you need strict 300ms p95 you can usually get there with INT8 + batching tuned.
[03:33] Aisha: That's promising. What's the expected variance between H100 and A100? We're running a mix across regions.
[03:40] Priya: H100 kernels are newer and tend to beat A100 by ~15-25% on throughput for the same quant profile; FP8 on H100 is especially good. A100 with INT8 still gives big wins but you might see slightly higher latencies. We can show side-by-side charts in the spreadsheet.
[04:00] Tom: For private deployments, how do we handle keys/KMS? Any change when we run quantized models?
[04:06] Jared: No change to KMS - quantization is a model transformation step and keys for customer data are still managed via your KMS/HSM as before. The private control plane just keeps telemetry and audit logs within your VPC.
[04:18] Marta: SOC 2, SSO - we have an audit starting in Q1, do you have SOC 2 docs we can share?
[04:24] Jared: Yes, will share SOC2 + ISO artifacts along with the security whitepaper in the next email.
[04:31] Priya: Back to performance - I want to show a quick live demo of the Optimize UI: we load your model (placeholder), run an automated quant sweep, and generate a profile that lists safe layers, recommended batch size, and expected p95.
[04:45] Priya: (screen share) Here in the console you can see a set of quant profiles - conservative, balanced, aggressive. Balanced is our default and often delivers the 1.8x throughput with <1% quality drop. Aggressive squeezes more latency but sometimes triggers fallback on specific prompts.
[05:10] Aisha: How often do you recommend re-profiling? We have weekly model updates during active dev.
[05:16] Priya: If model weights change meaningfully yes re-profile; for small optimizer or tokenizer tweaks it's usually stable, but we recommend running an automated smoke quant test as part of your CI for every release.
[05:28] Tom: About fallback - you mentioned automatic fallback policies. If a prompt is flagged as low confidence do you route it to fp16?
[05:36] Priya: Exactly - Optimize can insert a runtime guard: if the model confidence or a quality monitor threshold fails, request is either retried with fp16 or routed to a higher-fidelity model variant. That helps keep user experience stable while maximizing cost savings.
[05:51] Marta: Do we get raw token-level diffs to tune prompts? We want to identify what fails.
[05:56] Priya: Yes, in Redwood Console you can open the eval and see examples where quantized output diverged, with diffs and suggested rollbacks per prompt set.
[06:07] Aisha: Let's talk numbers for our production traffic. We do ~20k RT interactions per day, 60% are short chit-chat (<=64 tokens) and 40% are long summarization (avg 400 tokens). Will INT8 help on both?
[06:22] Priya: Short chats benefit mostly from lower per-token compute latency and batching; long summarization benefits a lot from KV cache and reduced memory foot print so you avoid model sharding. For your profile, hybrid approach makes sense - balanced INT8 for chat, maybe conservative or fp16 for the long summarizations that are quality sensitive.
[06:41] Tom: Any changes required to our serving infra? We're on Kubernetes with custom autoscaler.
[06:46] Priya: No major infra changes. For private deployments we provide a container runtime that exposes the same API. You'll need to have the quantized model artifact and the runtime image; autoscaler settings might be tightened for the new throughput numbers but it's mostly parameter tuning. We'll provide an Ops runbook.
[07:04] Aisha: What's the typical pilot duration you recommend?
[07:07] Jared: Our standard is a 1-2 week pilot with your eval prompts and ~48-72 hours of traffic replay on a staging H100 cluster; that gives statistically significant numbers. Then a short canary in prod for a few hours.
[07:20] Marta: For billing, do we get separate line items for Optimize tooling vs inference tokens?
[07:25] Jared: Yes - hosted inference billing remains per-token; Optimize has a small one-time onboarding or pilot fee for enterprise pilots and then it's included in Dedicated / Private packages depending on contract. We'll send the pricing sheet.
[07:36] Priya: I'll show one example of a quant sweep result - here the profile shows INT8 disabled for the attention-softmax layer for safety, but enabled elsewhere. The UI also shows expected p95 improvements and a quality delta column.
[07:52] Aisha: If we wanted to be aggressive, what delta are we likely to see?
[07:56] Priya: Aggressive profiles can push up to 3x throughput but quality delta can spike to 3-4% on sensitive benchmarks; that's why we recommend pilot and selective fallback.
[08:08] Tom: Any pre-built CI hooks? We use GitHub Actions.
[08:12] Priya: Yes, we have a test harness GitHub repo and a small action that runs the quant smoke tests and uploads results to a Redwood report URL. I'll include the repo link.
[08:22] Jared: Next, a couple of operational notes: we can do both host-side quant transforms or we can ship quantized artifacts for you to store. If you prefer on-prem artifacts, we sign an artifact manifest and you control distribution.
[08:39] Marta: That helps for our compliance folks.
[08:42] Aisha: Ok last part - success criteria for us: 1) keep summarization ROUGE within 1% of baseline, 2) p95 under 300ms for chat, 3) no production incidents during canary. If we meet that, we'll consider a Dedicated commit.
[09:00] Jared: Great, we'll aim to map the pilot to those success criteria.
[09:05] Priya: Quick Q&A - maybe 10 minutes.
[09:09] Tom: On the topic of quant artifacts, how are versioned? We want reproducible rollbacks.
[09:15] Priya: Each quant profile is a named artifact with model SHA + profile version; Console shows the artifact history and you can pin a run. Rollbacks are a single API call.
[09:24] Aisha: Sounds good. Can you share a sample pilot plan?
[09:28] Jared: Yes, action item for me to send pilot plan + pricing + SOC2.
[09:32] Marta: We'll try to get the eval set to you by Monday.
[09:35] Priya: I'll send the test harness link and a recommended config for H100 - batch sizes and kv cache settings that matched our examples.
[09:44] Aisha: One last clarifying thing - you mentioned automatic fallback based on confidence; how do you calculate confidence?
[09:50] Priya: It's model-proxy level heuristics - perplexity proxies, token-level logits, and a small learned classifier for hallucination signals. We provide default thresholds but you can tune them.
[10:03] Aisha: Good. Thanks everyone, this was useful.
[10:08] Jared: Thanks all - we'll follow up with the artifacts and schedule the pilot.
